scenes.tts: How do you show that a protein keeps neurons alive? You add it, and you take it away. Each test shows something different.
scenes.visual: Title card: Add It, Take It Away. A plus sign and a minus sign beside a ganglion.
scenes.narration: How do you show that a protein keeps neurons alive? You add it, and you take it away. Each test shows something different.

scenes.tts: A mouse tumour grafted into a chick embryo drew in sensory and sympathetic fibres. Stanley Cohen purified the activity as a protein.
scenes.visual: A chick embryo with a grafted tumour and fibres growing into it. Then a tube labelled purified protein. Credit: Cohen.
scenes.narration: A mouse tumour grafted into a chick embryo drew in sensory and sympathetic fibres. Stanley Cohen purified the activity as a protein.

scenes.tts: The question here is what that protein does in a normal animal.
scenes.visual: Question on screen: what does it do in a normal animal?
scenes.narration: The question here is what that protein does in a normal animal.

scenes.tts: Two words do the work. A factor is sufficient if it is enough, by itself, to produce an effect.
scenes.visual: Definition card: sufficient, enough by itself to produce an effect.
scenes.narration: Two words do the work. A factor is sufficient if it is enough, by itself, to produce an effect.

scenes.tts: It is necessary if the effect does not happen without it. Each experiment tests one of these, and no more.
scenes.visual: Definition card: necessary, no effect without it. The two cards sit side by side.
scenes.narration: It is necessary if the effect does not happen without it. Each experiment tests one of these, and no more.

scenes.tts: Sufficiency first. In nineteen sixty, Rita Levi-Montalcini and Barbara Booker gave the purified protein to young mammals.
scenes.caption: Sufficiency first. In 1960, Rita Levi-Montalcini and Barbara Booker gave the purified protein to young mammals.
scenes.visual: Credit: Levi-Montalcini and Booker, 1960. A young mouse schematic receiving an injection.
scenes.narration: Sufficiency first. In 1960, Rita Levi-Montalcini and Barbara Booker gave the purified protein to young mammals.

scenes.tts: Their sympathetic ganglia were greatly enlarged. Injected into chick embryos, the factor makes sensory and sympathetic ganglia overgrow.
scenes.visual: The sympathetic chain swells. Then a chick embryo whose sensory and sympathetic ganglia swell. Label: sufficiency.
scenes.narration: Their sympathetic ganglia were greatly enlarged. Injected into chick embryos, the factor makes sensory and sympathetic ganglia overgrow.

scenes.tts: A bigger ganglion does not say whether neurons were saved or born. That needs counts, which come later.
scenes.visual: A bigger ganglion with two arrows into it: saved? born? Label: needs counts.
scenes.narration: A bigger ganglion does not say whether neurons were saved or born. That needs counts, which come later.

scenes.tts: Now necessity. Cohen raised an antiserum, serum containing antibodies against one molecule. It blocked N G F's activity in culture.
scenes.caption: Now necessity. Cohen raised an antiserum, serum containing antibodies against one molecule. It blocked NGF's activity in culture.
scenes.visual: Y-shaped antibodies binding NGF and blocking it in a culture dish. Label: antiserum.
scenes.narration: Now necessity. Cohen raised an antiserum, serum containing antibodies against one molecule. It blocked NGF's activity in culture.

scenes.tts: Levi-Montalcini and Booker injected it into newborn mice, with rats and other mammals for comparison.
scenes.visual: A newborn mouse schematic receiving antiserum; small rat and other mammal icons beside it, labelled comparison.
scenes.narration: Levi-Montalcini and Booker injected it into newborn mice, with rats and other mammals for comparison.

scenes.tts: The sympathetic ganglia were destroyed. The procedure became known as immuno-sympathectomy.
scenes.caption: The sympathetic ganglia were destroyed. The procedure became known as immunosympathectomy.
scenes.visual: The sympathetic chain shrinks away. The word immunosympathectomy on screen. Label: necessity.
scenes.narration: The sympathetic ganglia were destroyed. The procedure became known as immunosympathectomy.

scenes.tts: Predict. Give the same antiserum to older animals. Does it destroy their sympathetic ganglia too?
scenes.visual: An age slider moves from newborn toward older. Question card: same effect?
scenes.narration: Predict. Give the same antiserum to older animals. Does it destroy their sympathetic ganglia too?

scenes.tts: It has much less effect. Dependence on N G F is tied to a developmental window.
scenes.caption: It has much less effect. Dependence on NGF is tied to a developmental window.
scenes.visual: As the slider moves to older ages, the shrinking effect weakens. Label: a window of dependence.
scenes.narration: It has much less effect. Dependence on NGF is tied to a developmental window.

scenes.tts: And the window differs between populations. N G F dependent sensory neurons are hit hardest by earlier exposure.
scenes.caption: And the window differs between populations. NGF dependent sensory neurons are hit hardest by earlier exposure.
scenes.visual: Two windows on a timeline: sensory neurons earlier, sympathetic neurons around birth. Schematic, no dates.
scenes.narration: And the window differs between populations. NGF dependent sensory neurons are hit hardest by earlier exposure.

scenes.tts: But an antiserum carries a doubt. It might kill neurons by binding something on them other than N G F.
scenes.caption: But an antiserum carries a doubt. It might kill neurons by binding something on them other than NGF.
scenes.visual: An antibody drifts off NGF and onto a different shape on the neuron surface. Label: the specificity doubt.
scenes.narration: But an antiserum carries a doubt. It might kill neurons by binding something on them other than NGF.

scenes.tts: So how would you remove N G F without using an antibody at all?
scenes.caption: So how would you remove NGF without using an antibody at all?
scenes.visual: Question card: remove NGF with no antibody?
scenes.narration: So how would you remove NGF without using an antibody at all?

scenes.tts: Takeaway: adding N G F is enough to enlarge the ganglia. Taking it away shows it is necessary, if the antibody is clean.
scenes.caption: Takeaway: adding NGF is enough to enlarge the ganglia. Taking it away shows it is necessary, if the antibody is clean.
scenes.visual: Closing card with two rows: add it, enough to enlarge the ganglia (saved or born still open); take it away, necessary (if the antibody is clean).
scenes.narration: Takeaway: adding NGF is enough to enlarge the ganglia. Taking it away shows it is necessary, if the antibody is clean.

scenes.visual: A gene diagram appears with a cross through one segment.
